title: Kat Butterfield & Daniel Audritt On Finding the Humor for a Man's Last Days Stuck in a Time Loop for 'Life Goes On'
excerpt: Daniel Audritt & Kat Butterfield discuss finding the right pace for balancing the heart and humor of 'Life Goes On'
content:
Are we obsessed with the concept of time? Losing it, filling it, not having enough of it? It’s a painful truth, in almost all of us, that we never think we have used our time wisely even if we are conscious of making sure that we value the time that we have with the ones we love. In Kat Butterfield and Daniel Audritt’s comforting and affirming short film, Life Goes On, a man has accepted his end just in time for an unusual circumstance to open his eyes to the beauty and humor in the little things in life.

Bill Bancroft is ready to go. His hospice bed creaks to life every morning only to see the same people in his large room in their own beds and the same cheery staff trying to brighten everyone’s morning. When a nurse asks him if he is comfortable, Bill replies, “Lap of luxury in here…five-star death experience.” Crotchety is one thing, but it takes on an entirely new meaning with David Bradley embodying the role. With his sneering lip, squinting eyes and dry delivery, Bradley is given the role of a lifetime.

Audritt and Butterfield’s mischievous screenplay takes a turn early on when Bill realizes that he’s stuck in a time loop of his final days. The same visitors arrive to tell the same boring stories. The same birthday cake is presented to one of his fellow bedmates on her special day. The same hopeful employee asks Bill if he can take his picture for the hospice newsletter–a delightfully cringey touch that has a real connection to the filmmaking pair. As Bill begins every same day anew, something about him softens–the small details filling in the crevices of his creaky annoyance.

Butterfield and Audritt’s film targets your heart with a light hand. Notice how they chart the speed of not just Bill’s hilariously slow bed but also the energy of everyone around him. Even though they are stuck in the same day, it feels like Bill is being shaken awake from being outside in the cold for too long. Finding the joy in the same day–for both the characters and the directors–poses their own unique problems, but this directorial effort is so nimble, fun, and, memorable.

Life Goes On never assumes to hold all the answers to the meaning of life, but it asks you to consider how you find the joy in living it.

Joey Moser
